entities.summary:
Guillaume de Pierre Godin, a prominent French Dominican theologian and cardinal, emerged as a significant figure during the tumultuous early 14th century, a period defined by the Avignon Papacy and profound shifts in ecclesiastical power. Born in Bayonne (exact date unknown), his career culminated in his death on June 12, 1336. Godin's intellectual prowess and administrative capabilities placed him at the heart of papal governance and theological discourse, particularly under Popes Clement V and John XXII, where he championed papal authority amidst conflicts with secular rulers and internal Church reform movements.

Godin's distinguished career began within the Dominican Order, where he earned a Master of Theology degree at the University of Paris. He served as provincial of the Dominican province of Provence before being appointed Master of the Sacred Palace, the Pope's personal theologian, a role he held from 1306 to 1312. Pope Clement V elevated him to Cardinal-Priest of Santa Cecilia in 1312, subsequently appointing him Cardinal-Bishop of Sabina in 1317. His responsibilities included critical legatine missions, such as to Sicily in 1312 and later to France to address disputes between the French crown and the Church, demonstrating his diplomatic skill and commitment to papal interests. He was also involved in the post-mortem proceedings against the Knights Templar.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Guillaume Pierre Godin was a key figure in reinforcing papal authority during the Avignon Papacy, contributing significantly to theological justifications and administrative strength of the Church. His work helped shape the relationship between spiritual and temporal powers in 14th-century Europe.
